title: Fit a circlip into its shaft groove with circlip pliers: spread it just enough, seat it square, turn it to check
instruction: Fit the retaining ring into the groove on the shaft with the circlip pliers, then put the pliers down.
context: Industrial machinery mechanics, maintenance technicians and machine assemblers (O*NET 49-9041.00, 51-2031.00) fit external retaining rings, or circlips, that keep gears and bearings on shafts. The ring is spread with circlip pliers in its two lug holes only as far as it takes to pass over the shaft, slid to its groove and let close into it, then turned in the groove to check it is seated all round. Ring makers give a maximum installation spread because spring steel opened past it takes a permanent set: the ring then sits loose in its groove and can walk out under load, so it is scrapped. A ring let go short of the groove grips the shaft in the wrong place, and one let go tilted lands half in the groove. Here the ring holds a spur gear on a 40 mm shaft.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A cast-iron fixture is fixed to the table: a base plate 12 x 12 x 1.2 cm centered at x 36, y -10, with a round bearing housing 6.4 cm across and 3.8 cm tall on it. A ground steel shaft 40 mm in diameter stands upright on the axis x 36, y -10, its end face 10.5 cm above the table with a 1.5 mm chamfer. A steel spur gear (56 mm across, 30 teeth, 1.6 cm thick) sits on the shaft from z 5.0 to 6.6. Just above the gear the shaft has a retaining-ring groove 1.85 mm wide with a 37.5 mm bottom diameter (DIN 471 for 40 mm), its lower wall flush with the gear's top face, from z 6.6 to 6.78. The ring is a DIN 471 external retaining ring for a 40 mm shaft, spring steel with a bright yellow zinc-chromate plating, 1.75 mm thick, 4.5 mm wide, free bore 36.5 mm, with two lug holes 12 mm apart; it lies flat on the shaft's end face, lugs toward the robot (at x 33.6). Its bore grows by (lug spacing - 12 mm) / pi: it clears the shaft from 40.2 mm (lug spacing 23.6 mm). The circlip pliers are external pliers with 90-degree bent tips, 13 cm long and 130 g: red handle grips 8 x 1.0 x 1.2 cm, 4.0 cm apart outside at rest; steel jaws crossing at a rivet; tips 1.7 cm long and 2.6 mm thick, 12 mm apart at rest. Squeezing the handles 1 mm closer spreads the tips 1 mm, up to an 18 mm stop. They lie along x on a black rubber rest block (8 x 3 x 3 cm, centered x 25.6, y -22), handles on the block with the grip point at x 26.1, y -22, z 3.6, tips toward +x hanging past the block's end at x 33.6.
scoring: Scored at the end of the run, with the ring's history kept over the whole run. Over-spread: if the ring's bore ever exceeded 41.0 mm (lug spacing 26.1 mm), 1 mm (2.5%) over the shaft, the usual maximum installation spread for this ring, it has taken a set and the score is 0, irreversible. Twisting its ends more than 10 degrees out of its plane (2.1 mm across the 12 mm lug spacing; ring makers say never twist a ring) for two control steps in a row is also 0, so a one-step jolt of the pliers in the sim doesn't count. Seated means the ring lies in the groove, closed onto its 37.5 mm bottom, out of the pliers, and not cocked: closed into the groove (however slowly) while tilted more than 4 degrees, its far side sits 3.4 mm off the groove plane, nearly twice the groove width, and lands on the shaft beside it. Put down means the pliers are out of the ring, no gripper holds them (fingers closed with the tool point within 3 cm of the pliers anywhere from handle butt to tips), and they lie still over the bench, grip point from 1 cm below to 5 cm above its top (not on the floor). Not seated or pliers not put down: 0. Seated and put down: 0.5; 1.0 if the ring's net turn in its groove is also at least 15 degrees (5 mm at its rim), the check that it is free all round; net is the span between the smallest and largest angle it reached there, so wiggling back and forth counts only the wiggle's width. Full score also needs both arms home and still (tool points within 3 cm of their start); otherwise 0.9. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. A real trial is checked from the top video (lug spacing against a mm scale on the plate), a straightedge on the gear face at four points, and a paint mark on the ring against one on the shaft.
reset_notes: Take the ring off with the pliers (spread no more than 41 mm), check its free bore with calipers and replace it if it measures over 36.6 mm, lay it on the shaft's end face with the lugs toward the robot, and put the pliers back on the rest block.
fidelity: The ring has no contact simulation: its position along the shaft, turn and bore are a model driven by the pliers' tips once both are in its lug holes (it slides only when spread past the shaft, closes into the groove when let go over it), with DIN 471 sizes. It has no collision shape, so only the pliers move it. The pliers' jaws are a crossed slide, so handle and tip travel are 1:1. Tilt and twist come from the pliers' pose.
